scoring.formula: raw[axis] = sum(mult * effect[axis]); max[axis] = sum(abs(effect[axis])); score[axis] = 100 * (max + raw) / (2 * max)

meta.presentation: Stored grouped by axis for maintainability. The app must SHUFFLE at runtime with a fixed seed so consecutive items do not come from the same axis.

axes.posPole: No Support for Any National Struggle

questions.text: Revolutionary consciousness arises from the class's own activity, not from a party that brings it in from outside.
Councils elected and recallable on the shop floor are the only legitimate organs of proletarian power.
Fixed leadership positions reproduce the separation between leaders and led that the revolution exists to abolish.
Delegation should be so immediate and revocable that no delegate ever becomes a fixture.
The class does not need a general staff; it needs to recognise its own power.
Organisational forms should dissolve back into the class the moment their task is done.
A single centralised organisation, organically unified around one programme, is what turns scattered militancy into a revolution.
Without a party the class can win a strike, but not a revolution.
Discipline flowing from an organic centre is a strength, not a defect, of a revolutionary organisation.
Councils without a party to give them a programme drift and dissolve.
Centralism is not the enemy of the working class; disorganisation is.
The organisation exists prior to and independent of the immediate mood of the class, and must.
The programme should be rewritten as the movement's practice reveals new possibilities.
No text handed down from an earlier period can bind revolutionaries in the present.
Theory develops through the struggle itself, not through fidelity to a founding document.
A programme fixed in the past cannot anticipate the forms communisation will actually take.
Openness to revision is a sign of a living theory, not of opportunism.
Each cycle of struggles produces its own theoretical questions that earlier texts could not have posed.
The invariant core of the communist programme was established long ago and cannot be revised without abandoning it.
What looks like theoretical innovation is usually the old opportunism finding new words.
A movement that keeps revising its basic positions has no basis on which to build continuity.
The party's theses are the fixed compass by which every new development is judged.
Adapting the programme to the mood of the moment is how revolutionary movements are lost.
Loyalty to the founding texts is what distinguishes a real communist current from its impostors.
The abolition of value, wage labour, and the state must begin immediately, in the revolution itself, not after a transition.
Waiting for a workers' state to wither away has always meant the state does not wither.
Communism is a set of immediate measures, not a distant end-state to be built toward.
Any period of continued wage labour under a revolutionary government reproduces capitalist social relations.
The revolution either abolishes exchange at the outset or it isn't a communist revolution at all.
Producing for need rather than for exchange has to start on day one, not after a period of accumulation.
A transitional period of workers' state power is necessary before value and wage labour can be abolished.
Trying to abolish exchange immediately, before production has developed, produces only generalised scarcity.
The dictatorship of the proletariat is a real stage, not a formula to be skipped over.
Communism has to be built up through planned development, not declared into existence overnight.
Without a period of proletarian state power, the old ruling class simply retakes what was taken from it.
The idea that communism can be achieved in a single stroke underestimates what it takes to reorganise production.
Reproducing daily life outside the wage relation is as much a terrain of struggle as the factory floor.
The revolution has to transform housework, care, and consumption, not just the point of production.
Struggles in the neighbourhood and the household are not secondary to the strike; they are part of the same struggle.
Capital organises life outside the workplace as thoroughly as it organises work, and both have to be contested.
A revolution that changes ownership of the factories but leaves domestic and social reproduction untouched has changed less than it thinks.
The community, not only the workplace, is where the working class actually lives its condition.
The wage relation at the point of production is the foundation everything else rests on; struggles elsewhere are secondary to it.
Whoever controls production controls the rest of social life as a consequence.
Focusing on lifestyle and everyday life is a retreat from the discipline of class struggle at work.
The factory remains the decisive site because that is where surplus value is actually extracted.
Struggles over consumption and daily life rarely generalise the way strikes at the point of production do.
Organising the workplace is harder and more decisive than organising the neighbourhood, and should be prioritised.
Trade unions today function to manage and contain working-class discontent on capital's behalf.
A union's job is to negotiate the price of labour power, which means administering exploitation, not ending it.
Union bureaucracies have interests of their own that diverge from the rank and file's.
The more successfully a union is integrated into collective bargaining, the less capable it is of revolutionary action.
Permanent union structures tend to outlive their usefulness and become obstacles to wildcat action.
Workers acting outside and against their own unions is sometimes the only way forward.
Mass unions remain the indispensable organisational vehicle through which the working class builds its power.
Abandoning the unions cedes the largest existing workers' organisations to the class enemy for nothing.
Building rank-and-file strength inside the unions is more realistic than trying to bypass them.
A union, whatever its bureaucracy's faults, still organises workers on a scale nothing else does.
Syndicalist strategy has a real record of building working-class power that dismissing the unions ignores.
Even a compromised union is a better base for organising than none at all.
Standing candidates for parliament can be used to build revolutionary organisation and propaganda even without illusions in the state.
Winning a parliamentary majority is one legitimate route among others to transforming society.
Revolutionaries should use every legal opening, including elections, that helps organise the class.
A seat in parliament gives a platform that street agitation alone cannot reach.
Refusing all engagement with representative institutions cuts revolutionaries off from millions of workers who still vote.
Participating in elections tactically does not commit a movement to parliamentary illusions.
Parliament is a capitalist institution that cannot be used for revolutionary ends, however tactically it is approached.
Voting confirms the fiction that the state represents the interests of those it rules over.
Every experience of workers' parties entering parliament has ended in their absorption into the system.
Abstention from elections is a matter of principle, not a tactic to be weighed case by case.
A revolutionary organisation that contests elections has already accepted the terrain the state has set for it.
Direct action outside all institutional channels is the only form of politics that hasn't been recuperated.
Anti-colonial and national liberation struggles deserve support as blows against imperialism, whatever their internal class content.
Backing a national liberation movement against a colonial power is a defensible tactical choice for internationalists.
National liberation struggles, whatever their limits, weaken the world system revolutionaries are trying to overthrow.
Solidarity with the colonised is owed even when the movement leading the struggle is not itself communist.
Refusing to distinguish coloniser from colonised in the name of pure class politics ends up serving the coloniser.
A national liberation struggle can be a genuine front of the wider struggle against capital.
The nation is a bourgeois category, and no national struggle, colonial or otherwise, is a proletarian one.
Support for national liberation always ends up subordinating class struggle to a new nationalist ruling class.
Every national liberation movement in power has built a new state that exploits its own working class.
Internationalism means refusing all national flags, including those raised against colonialism.
A struggle organised around the nation cannot, by its nature, point toward the abolition of classes.
Solidarity should go to the proletariat inside a colonised country, never to the movement claiming to speak for the nation as a whole.
Mass strikes that draw in the whole class are the movement's most powerful weapon.
The revolution will be made by the broad movement of the class, not by any smaller group acting on its behalf.
A generalised strike, spreading through solidarity rather than leadership, is the model of revolutionary action.
Building toward a mass strike is more valuable than any isolated action a small group could carry out.
The class moves as a class or it doesn't move at all; there is no substitute for its numbers.
Wide participation, even if less disciplined, beats a small group's more coordinated action.
Small groups willing to act decisively can break an impasse that a mass movement, waiting for consensus, cannot.
Riot, sabotage, and expropriation are legitimate tactics regardless of whether the broader class is yet moving.
Waiting for a mass movement to arrive before acting means never acting at all.
A determined minority that acts can open possibilities a passive majority never would have found on its own.
Direct, immediate action matters more than building the numbers for a hypothetical future mass strike.
Insurrectionary action doesn't need to wait for the working class as a whole to be ready.
